Godzilla is built from three ideas that compose into everything else in these docs. Understanding how they relate makes the rest of the platform — guides, API reference, SDKs — much easier to follow.

{{ds:component/card|href={{cms:item/614fa99d-e5a6-43da-ba0c-d01c2c498a56}}|tag=Concept|title=Pipelines|description=Named, versioned workflows that move data from a source to a destination through optional transforms.}} {{ds:component/card|href={{cms:item/f9b148b3-dc03-4657-8f05-4d79cc5634af}}|tag=Concept|title=Connectors|description=Pre-built integrations to external systems — sources, destinations, or both.}} {{ds:component/card|href={{cms:item/1422591b-2a03-40ca-8137-48fa50fe0e74}}|tag=Concept|title=Events|description=The atomic unit of data flowing through a pipeline, plus the platform's own lifecycle events.}}

How they fit together

A pipeline reads events from a source connector, transforms them, and writes them to a destination connector. Everything else in Godzilla — retries, webhooks, monitoring — is built on top of that single loop.

Working with events

Once you understand the core three, two supporting concepts make pipelines more robust:

{{ds:component/card|href={{cms:item/ee6f8392-705c-41e5-b4f4-442c4817a3a1}}|tag=Concept|title=Schemas|description=Declare and validate the shape of event payloads, catching data corruption early before it propagates downstream.}}

Glossary

Short definitions for every term used throughout these docs.

Pipeline
A named, versioned workflow that moves data from a source connector, through optional transforms, to a destination connector.
Connector
A pre-built integration to an external system — a source, a destination, or both.
Event
The atomic unit of data moving through a pipeline, or a platform lifecycle notification like pipeline.failed.
Webhook
An outbound HTTP request Godzilla sends to a URL you control when a subscribed event occurs.
Dead-letter queue
Where an event goes after exhausting its retries, rather than being dropped. See Error handling & recovery.
Cursor pagination
The pagination style used by every v2 list endpoint. See Limits, quotas & errors.
Workspace
The top-level account boundary an API key is scoped to.

{{ds:component/hero|title=Concepts|subtitle=The three building blocks every Godzilla pipeline is made of.|cta_html=Start with Pipelines}}

Godzilla is built from three ideas that compose into everything else in these docs. Understanding how they relate makes the rest of the platform — guides, API reference, SDKs — much easier to follow.

{{ds:component/card|href={{cms:item/614fa99d-e5a6-43da-ba0c-d01c2c498a56}}|tag=Concept|title=Pipelines|description=Named, versioned workflows that move data from a source to a destination through optional transforms.}} {{ds:component/card|href={{cms:item/f07cfc56-e541-428b-af08-64b28bfc4505}}|tag=Concept|title=Connectors|description=Pre-built integrations to external systems — sources, destinations, or both.}} {{ds:component/card|href={{cms:item/e66cc8b1-5b0c-45aa-bd48-343c6b1709a7}}|tag=Concept|title=Events|description=The atomic unit of data flowing through a pipeline, plus the platform's own lifecycle events.}}

How they fit together

A pipeline reads events from a source connector, transforms them, and writes them to a destination connector. Everything else in Godzilla — retries, webhooks, monitoring — is built on top of that single loop.

Working with events

Once you understand the core three, two supporting concepts make pipelines more robust:

{{ds:component/card|href={{cms:item/ee6f8392-705c-41e5-b4f4-442c4817a3a1}}|tag=Concept|title=Schemas|description=Declare and validate the shape of event payloads, catching data corruption early before it propagates downstream.}}

Glossary

Short definitions for every term used throughout these docs.

Pipeline
A named, versioned workflow that moves data from a source connector, through optional transforms, to a destination connector.
Connector
A pre-built integration to an external system — a source, a destination, or both.
Event
The atomic unit of data moving through a pipeline, or a platform lifecycle notification like pipeline.failed.
Webhook
An outbound HTTP request Godzilla sends to a URL you control when a subscribed event occurs.
Dead-letter queue
Where an event goes after exhausting its retries, rather than being dropped. See Error handling & recovery.
Cursor pagination
The pagination style used by every v2 list endpoint. See Rate limits.
Workspace
The top-level account boundary an API key is scoped to.

Building your first pipeline

This guide walks through creating a pipeline end to end: a source connector, a destination connector, and the pipeline that ties them together.

{{ds:component/alert|variant=info|title=Before you start|body_html=

You'll need an API key. See Authentication in Getting Started if you don't have one yet.

}} {{ds:component/docs-toc|items_html=

  • 2. Create a destination connector
  • 3. Create the pipeline
  • Next steps
    • }}

    1. Create a source connector

    We'll pull orders from Postgres. See Connectors for the full catalog of types.

    {{ds:component/code-block|filename=create-source.sh|language=bash|code=curl -X POST https://api.godzilladocs.dev/v2/connectors \ -H "Authorization: Bearer $GODZILLA_API_KEY" \ -d '{"type":"postgres","direction":"source","config":{"connection_string":"postgres://..."}}'}} {{ds:component/code-block|filename=create_source.go|language=go|code=package main import ( "context" "log" "os" "github.com/godzilladev/godzilla-go" ) func main() { client := godzilla.NewClient( godzilla.WithAPIKey(os.Getenv("GODZILLA_API_KEY")), ) connector, err := client.Connectors.Create(context.Background(), &godzilla.CreateConnectorRequest{ Type: "postgres", Direction: "source", Config: map[string]interface{}{ "connection_string": "postgres://...", }, }) if err != nil { log.Fatalf("failed to create connector: %v", err) } log.Printf("Created connector: %s ", connector.ID) }}}

    2. Create a destination connector

    We'll write to Snowflake.

    {{ds:component/code-block|filename=create-destination.sh|language=bash|code=curl -X POST https://api.godzilladocs.dev/v2/connectors \ -H "Authorization: Bearer $GODZILLA_API_KEY" \ -d '{"type":"snowflake","direction":"destination","config":{"account":"..."}}'}} {{ds:component/code-block|filename=create_destination.go|language=go|code=package main import ( "context" "log" "os" "github.com/godzilladev/godzilla-go" ) func main() { client := godzilla.NewClient( godzilla.WithAPIKey(os.Getenv("GODZILLA_API_KEY")), ) connector, err := client.Connectors.Create(context.Background(), &godzilla.CreateConnectorRequest{ Type: "snowflake", Direction: "destination", Config: map[string]interface{}{ "account": "...", }, }) if err != nil { log.Fatalf("failed to create connector: %v", err) } log.Printf("Created connector: %s ", connector.ID) }}}

    3. Create the pipeline

    Full request/response details are in the Pipelines endpoint reference.

    {{ds:component/code-block|filename=create-pipeline.sh|language=bash|code=curl -X POST https://api.godzilladocs.dev/v2/pipelines \ -H "Authorization: Bearer $GODZILLA_API_KEY" \ -d '{"name":"ingest-orders","source_connector_id":"conn_pg_orders","destination_connector_id":"conn_snowflake_dw"}'}} {{ds:component/code-block|filename=create_pipeline.go|language=go|code=package main import ( "context" "log" "os" "github.com/godzilladev/godzilla-go" ) func main() { client := godzilla.NewClient( godzilla.WithAPIKey(os.Getenv("GODZILLA_API_KEY")), ) pipeline, err := client.Pipelines.Create(context.Background(), &godzilla.CreatePipelineRequest{ Name: "ingest-orders", SourceConnectorID: "conn_pg_orders", DestinationConnectorID: "conn_snowflake_dw", }) if err != nil { log.Fatalf("failed to create pipeline: %v", err) } log.Printf("Created pipeline: %s ", pipeline.ID) }}}

    The pipeline starts in draft state. Activate it once you're ready to start processing events.

    Next steps

    Now that events are flowing, read Handling errors & retries to see what happens when a write fails, or Monitoring & alerts to watch it run.

Error handling & recovery

Every event that fails a transform or a destination write is retried automatically. This guide covers how that works and what to do when retries run out.

{{ds:component/docs-toc|items_html=
  • Automatic retries
  • Dead-lettering
  • Replaying events
  • Watching for failures
    • }}

    Automatic retries

    Failed events retry with exponential backoff — 1s, 2s, 4s, up to a per-pipeline configurable ceiling. Most transient failures (a destination hiccup, a rate-limited third party) resolve within the first few attempts.

    {{ds:component/code-block|filename=pipeline-retry-config.json|language=json|code={ "retry_policy": { "max_attempts": 5, "backoff": "exponential", "initial_delay_ms": 1000 } }}}

    Dead-lettering

    An event that exhausts its retries is moved to that pipeline's dead-letter queue rather than dropped silently.

    {{ds:component/alert|variant=danger|title=Dead-lettered events don't retry themselves|body_html=

    Once in the dead-letter queue, an event stays there until you replay it or explicitly discard it — it will not retry again on its own.

    }}

    Replaying events

    Use the Events endpoint's replay action to re-run a specific dead-lettered event once the underlying issue is fixed.

    {{ds:component/code-block|filename=replay.sh|language=bash|code=curl -X POST https://api.godzilladocs.dev/v2/events/evt_8f2c1a90/replay \ -H "Authorization: Bearer $GODZILLA_API_KEY"}}

    Watching for failures

    Subscribe to pipeline.failed via Webhooks so you find out about dead-lettered events before a customer does. See also Monitoring & alerts.

Events

An event is the atomic unit of data that moves through a Pipeline. Every record a source connector emits, every row a transform produces, and every write a destination connector performs is an event.

Event shape

{{ds:component/code-block|filename=event.json|language=json|code={ "id": "evt_8f2c1a90", "type": "order.created", "occurred_at": "2026-08-18T09:12:44Z", "source": "connector_postgres_orders", "payload": { "order_id": "ord_4471", "amount_cents": 4899 } }}}

User data events vs. platform events

Godzilla distinguishes two kinds of events:

  • User data events — the records your pipelines process, shaped however your source system produces them.
  • Platform events — lifecycle notifications Godzilla itself emits: pipeline.started, pipeline.completed, pipeline.failed, connector.error. These are what power Webhooks.
{{ds:component/alert|variant=info|title=Ordering|body_html=

Events are delivered in-order per source partition, not globally. Two events from different source partitions may be processed out of order relative to each other.

}}

Payloads and schemas

The payload field in every event can be validated against a schema. A schema is a JSON Schema document that declares the expected structure, types, and constraints of your event payloads. Defining a schema for your pipeline helps catch malformed or unexpected data early, before it silently corrupts downstream systems.

See Schemas to learn how to declare one and enforce validation across all events in a pipeline.

Retries and dead-lettering

An event that fails a transform or destination write is retried with exponential backoff. After the configured retry limit, it is moved to that pipeline's dead-letter queue rather than dropped. See Handling errors & retries for how to configure and drain a dead-letter queue.

Query and replay events

Once events have flowed through a pipeline, you can query them, inspect their status, and replay dead-lettered events. See the Events endpoint API reference for how to list, filter, and replay events programmatically.

Assigning schemas to a pipeline

Once you've defined a schema, you attach it to a pipeline's payload type during pipeline creation or configuration. When you do, Godzilla validates the payload of every event (the payload field in each event object) against that schema.

If an event payload fails validation, the event is rejected with a validation error rather than being silently corrupted. You can inspect validation failures in the pipeline's error logs and metrics, and decide whether to:

  • New field: Add the field to properties. If you make it required, existing events must be updated before they can flow through. If optional, old events pass validation as-is.
